PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Swimming is an optional sub-strand for schools that can use a pool safely. You will learn how a pool is organised, how to enter feet first, and how to play simple water games. You will then practise the mushroom, supine and prone floats, and a glide, always with a teacher present and with safety rules in and out of the water.

## Strand 2.0: Performing and Displaying
Sub-strand 2.6: Swimming (Optional)
Suggested lessons: 15

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) recognise ways of water entry in the swimming pool
b) play water games in the swimming pool for fun
c) float in water for skill acquisition
d) glide in water for water confidence
e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## What this sub-strand covers
• Water entry
• Water games
• Floating technique- mushroom supine and prone
• Gliding

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why is Swimming an essential life skill?

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: The learner builds confidence by floating in water
• Learning to learn: The learner acquires the skills of pool entry and floating in water

## Values
• Respect: The learner respects others' performance in floating and gliding in water
• Responsibility: The learner observes own and others safety while performing and practising the water entry, floating and gliding

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Safety and security: The learner adheres to water safety precautions while practising water entry, floating and gliding
• Environmental awareness: The learner familiarises with the pool environment, safe use of water and pool hygiene

## Links to other learning areas
• Science and Technology: The learner develops a practical understanding of correct body posture when floating and gliding

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Creative Arts Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Performing and Displaying, Sub-strand 2.6 Swimming (Optional)

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Knowing the pool and why swimming matters

LESSON 1: KNOWING THE POOL AND WHY SWIMMING MATTERS
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Name the main parts of a swimming pool area.
• Explain why swimming is a life skill.
• State rules for moving safely on the pool deck.

Curriculum outcomes: a) recognise ways of water entry in the swimming pool; e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## Introduction
The edge of a pool is hard, and the water is not the same depth everywhere. Before anyone floats or plays, the class needs to know the place and the reasons for being careful.

## Notes
A swimming pool is a controlled place to learn water skills. This sub-strand is optional: it is taught where a pool and proper supervision are available. Do not practise these skills in a river, a dam, a well or flood water.

### Parts of the pool area
- The **deck** is the floor around the pool. It is often wet and slippery.
- **Steps or a ladder** are a safe way in and out.
- The **shallow end** is where your class learns. You should be able to stand with your head well above the water.
- The **deep end** is for swimmers the teacher has passed. Stay out of it in these lessons.
- A **lifeguard or teacher** watches the water. Their whistle means stop and look at them.
- **Lane ropes** and markers divide the water. Do not hang on ropes unless you are told to.

### Why swimming is a life skill
Water is part of ordinary life: baths, rain, rivers and pools. A person who can enter water calmly, float and reach the side has a better chance of staying safe if they fall in. Swimming also builds fitness, breath control and confidence. It is enjoyable. At Grade 4 you are beginning that skill, not training to rescue other people. If someone is in trouble, you shout for an adult. You do not jump in to be a hero.

### On the deck
Walk. Do not run, push or dive. Shower if the pool rules say so. Listen before you go near the edge. These habits are the start of safety in and out of the pool.

## Key words
• deck — the floor around the swimming pool
• shallow end — the part of the pool where you can stand safely
• life skill — a skill that can protect you in real life

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner runs along the wet deck. What is the danger, and what should they do instead?

Working:
1. Wet decks are slippery.
2. Running can cause a fall onto a hard surface or into the water.

Answer: They may slip and be hurt. They should walk.

### Example 2
Why is swimming called a life skill?

Working:
1. It helps a person stay safer in water.
2. It also builds fitness and confidence.

Answer: It helps you stay calm and safer if you are in water, and it keeps the body fit.

## Activity: Pool walk and rules
You will need: A supervised swimming pool, Whistle, Swim clothes
1. With the teacher, walk the deck and point to the shallow end, the deep end, the steps and the lifeguard’s place.
2. Practise stopping still when the whistle blows.
3. In pairs, say one reason swimming is a life skill.
4. Agree three deck rules and repeat them aloud.
5. Do not enter the water until the teacher gives the instruction.

## Practice
1. Where should Grade 4 beginners stay in the pool?
2. What does a whistle from the teacher or lifeguard mean?
3. Give two deck rules.

## Summary
• Learn the deck, the steps, the shallow end and the deep end.
• Swimming can keep you safer in water and makes you fitter.
• Walk on the deck and obey the whistle.

### Answers to practice
1. In the shallow end, where they can stand, with a teacher watching.
2. Stop and look at the adult.
3. Any two: walk, do not push, do not dive, listen to the adult, shower if required.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Entering the water feet first

LESSON 2: ENTERING THE WATER FEET FIRST
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Enter the pool using steps and a feet-first method.
• Explain why this class does not dive.
• Get out of the pool safely when told.

Curriculum outcomes: a) recognise ways of water entry in the swimming pool; e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## Introduction
How you enter the water is a skill of its own. In this class the rule is simple: feet first, and only where the teacher has told you to enter.

## Notes
There is more than one safe way into a pool. All of the ways you use now put the feet in first. You do not dive. Diving into water that is shallow, or into water you have not checked, can injure the head and the neck.

### Ways to enter
1. **Steps or ladder.** Face the steps, hold the rail, and walk down one step at a time until you are standing on the pool floor. This is the first method to master.
2. **Sitting entry.** Sit on the edge where the teacher shows you. Both hands hold the edge. Turn your body, slide in, and land on your feet. Keep your head up.
3. **Feet-first jump.** Use this only when the teacher points to a place where you can stand afterwards and where jumping is allowed. Bend your knees, look forward, jump so the feet go in first, and let the knees bend again as you land in the water. Do not leap far out into the pool. Do not jump onto another person.

Never enter by flipping, diving, or being pushed.

### Getting out
Swim or walk to the steps and climb out, or place both hands on the edge, push down and climb onto a knee. Do not pull on another learner. When the whistle says the turn is over, get out at once.

### Safety around entry
One person enters at a time at each entry point. Wait a body-length away from the person in front. Keep your eyes on the water where you will land. If you feel afraid, say so. Using the steps is a successful entry. Confidence grows from calm practice, not from a dare.

## Key words
• feet-first — entering the water with the feet going in before the head
• dive — going in head first; not allowed in these lessons

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The shallow end is busy and a friend says, “Dive at the deep end so you look brave.” What should you do?

Working:
1. This class enters feet first only.
2. The deep end is not the learning area.

Answer: Refuse. Enter feet first at the place the teacher has given you.

### Example 2
Three learners want to use the ladder at once. What is the safe number at a time?

Working:
1. One person enters at each entry point at a time.

Answer: One.

## Activity: Feet-first entries
You will need: Supervised pool, Steps or ladder, Teacher or lifeguard
1. Watch the teacher demonstrate the steps, the sitting entry and, if the depth is safe, a feet-first jump.
2. Enter one at a time by the steps and stand in the shallow water.
3. Get out and, if you are ready, practise the sitting entry.
4. Try a feet-first jump only where the teacher stands and only if you agree you are ready.
5. Climb out safely when the whistle blows.

## Practice
1. Name two feet-first ways to enter a pool.
2. Why do you not dive in this sub-strand?
3. How many learners should use the ladder at the same time?

## Summary
• Enter on the steps, by sliding in from sitting, or with a feet-first jump if allowed.
• Do not dive or push anyone in.
• Get out on the steps or by climbing onto a knee when told.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: steps or ladder, sitting entry, feet-first jump where the teacher allows it.
2. Diving is head first and can injure the head and neck, especially in shallow water.
3. One.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Water games for confidence

LESSON 3: WATER GAMES FOR CONFIDENCE
====================================

## What you will learn
• Play simple games in shallow water.
• Follow safety rules while playing.
• Explain how games help you feel at home in the water.

Curriculum outcomes: b) play water games in the swimming pool for fun; e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## Introduction
Games in shallow water are not a break from learning. They teach you to move, watch others and listen to the whistle while you are having fun.

## Notes
Water games in this lesson stay in the shallow end. You can stand up at any moment. An adult is watching. The games are for confidence and enjoyment, not for rough play.

### Game 1: Walk and greet
Walk across the shallow end, shoulders under the water if you are tall enough for that to be safe, and give a partner a calm high-five. Change direction when the whistle blows. This teaches you to move without grabbing.

### Game 2: Collect the floats
The teacher floats a few safe objects, such as balls, on the water. In turns, walk or paddle and bring one object back to the side. No diving down. If an object sinks, leave it for the teacher.

### Game 3: Statues
Move gently through the water until the whistle blows, then freeze. A freeze might be standing still, or holding the side. Pushing someone who is a statue is not part of the game.

### Safety inside the game
- Stay in the area the teacher marked.
- Keep your feet under you unless the teacher has asked for a float.
- Do not duck another person’s head under the water.
- Do not run on the spot so wildly that you slip.
- Leave the game the moment the whistle sounds, even if you are about to collect a ball.
- Help a friend who is nervous by staying near them, not by pulling them.

These games make the pool feel familiar. Familiar water is safer water, because you are not panicking at the cold, the splash or the space. Fun and safety are practised together.

## Key words
• water confidence — feeling calm and able to follow instructions in the water
• shallow-end game — a game played where you can stand safely

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During Collect the floats, a ball sinks. What should a learner do?

Working:
1. The lesson says not to dive down.
2. An adult collects sunken objects.

Answer: Leave it for the teacher. Do not dive down.

### Example 2
Why must the game stop when the whistle blows, even if you are winning?

Working:
1. The whistle is a safety signal.
2. Safety is more important than the point.

Answer: The whistle means stop and look at the adult. Safety comes before the game.

## Activity: Three shallow-water games
You will need: Supervised shallow water, Whistle, A few floating balls
1. Enter feet first and stand where you can touch the floor.
2. Play Walk and greet, stopping on the whistle.
3. Play Collect the floats in turns.
4. Play Statues without pushing.
5. Climb out, and tell a partner which game helped you feel calmer in the water.

## Practice
1. Name one water game for the shallow end.
2. What must you never do to another person’s head during a water game?
3. Why are water games useful?

## Summary
• Play in the shallow end where you can stand.
• Do not duck heads, dive for sunk objects, or ignore the whistle.
• Games make the water familiar and enjoyable.

### Answers to practice
1. Any one: Walk and greet, Collect the floats, or Statues.
2. Push it under the water.
3. They build confidence and enjoyment while you practise moving safely and listening.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: The mushroom float

LESSON 4: THE MUSHROOM FLOAT
============================

## What you will learn
• Describe the shape of a mushroom float.
• Practise the float in shallow water with support nearby.
• Stand up from the float with control.

Curriculum outcomes: c) float in water for skill acquisition

## Introduction
A mushroom float curls the body into a round shape so the water can hold you for a moment. It is often the first float learners trust, because the knees are tucked and the face is near the surface.

## Notes
Floating means resting in the water so the body is held up without standing. The mushroom float is also called a tuck float. The back rounds near the surface like the cap of a mushroom, and the knees are tucked underneath.

### How to do it
1. Stand in the shallow end where your feet can push the floor.
2. Take a breath.
3. Bend the knees and pull them toward the chest.
4. Hold the shins with the hands.
5. Round the back and let the body tip forward gently. The face may go into the water for a short moment if you are ready. If you are not ready, keep the chin near the water and the face to the side, and tell the teacher. Do not force the face in.
6. Stay tucked and relaxed. Tight, panicked muscles make you sink.
7. To stand: lift the head, press the feet down to the floor, and stand tall. The teacher or a partner may stand beside you, but they do not hold you under.

Practise near the side so you can touch it. One learner floats at a time in each small space. Count a short hold, such as three counts, then stand. As you improve, the hold can grow.

The mushroom float teaches you that water can support a calm body. It is a skill for confidence. It is not a test of how long you can stay without breath. If you need air, stand up at once.

## Key words
• mushroom float — a tucked float with the knees to the chest and the back rounded at the surface
• float — to rest in the water so it holds you up

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner holds a mushroom float for 3 counts, stands, and does it again for 3 counts. How many counts were spent floating?

Working:
1. 3 + 3 = 6

Answer: 6

### Example 2
A learner feels they need air during the float. What should they do?

Working:
1. Breath matters more than the hold.
2. The recovery is to stand.

Answer: Stand up at once by lifting the head and pressing the feet to the floor.

## Activity: Tuck and float
You will need: Shallow supervised water, Pool side within reach
1. Watch a demonstration of the mushroom float and the stand-up.
2. Hold the side, tuck the knees, and round the back for a short count.
3. Let go only if you feel ready, with a partner beside you but not holding you down.
4. Stand up with control.
5. Tell your partner one thing that helped you float.

## Practice
1. What shape is the body in a mushroom float?
2. How do you stand up from the float?
3. Should you force your face into the water if you are afraid?

## Summary
• Tuck the knees, hold the shins and round the back.
• Relax, hold briefly, then stand by pressing the feet down.
• Stay in shallow water and stop when you need air.

### Answers to practice
1. Tucked and round, knees to the chest, back near the surface.
2. Lift the head, press the feet to the floor and stand tall.
3. No. Keep the face to the side until you are ready, and tell the teacher.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: Supine and prone floats

LESSON 5: SUPINE AND PRONE FLOATS
=================================

## What you will learn
• Float on the back in a supine float.
• Float face down in a prone float, with a safe way to breathe.
• Compare the two body positions.

Curriculum outcomes: c) float in water for skill acquisition

## Introduction
The mushroom float tucks you into a ball. The next floats stretch you out. Supine means face up. Prone means face down. Both need a calm body and shallow water.

## Notes
### Supine float
Supine means lying on the back.

1. Hold the pool side with both hands, arms bent.
2. Lift the hips and let the chest rise so the ears rest in the water.
3. Look up at the sky or the roof, not at your feet. Looking at the feet makes the hips sink.
4. When you are ready, let the arms float out to the sides, like a letter T.
5. Keep the legs relaxed. A small kick is allowed if the teacher has shown it, but the aim is to rest, not to race.
6. Breathe normally. The mouth stays clear of the water.
7. To stand: tuck the knees, bring the head forward and press the feet down.

### Prone float
Prone means face down, on the front.

1. Face the side and hold it.
2. Take a breath and place the face in the water if you are ready, arms stretched forward or out.
3. Let the legs trail. The body is long, a little like a star if the arms and legs are spread.
4. To breathe, lift the head or turn it to the side, or stand up.
5. Do not stay face down if you feel short of air.

### What the two floats teach
Supine lets you breathe more easily, so many learners gain confidence there first. Prone teaches you to put the face in and to stretch long, which you will need for a front glide. In both, a tight, frightened body sinks faster than a relaxed one. Practise beside the side, one person in each space, with the teacher watching.

Science link: a long, level body lies better on the water than a body folded at the hips. Posture is part of floating.

## Key words
• supine float — a back float, face up
• prone float — a front float, face down

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During a back float, a learner looks down toward the toes and the hips sink. What should they look at?

Working:
1. Looking at the feet drops the hips.
2. The eyes should look up.

Answer: They should look up, with the ears in the water.

### Example 2
Which float makes breathing easier for a beginner, supine or prone? Why?

Working:
1. Supine is face up.
2. The mouth can stay out of the water.

Answer: Supine, because the face is up and the mouth can stay clear of the water.

## Activity: Back float and front float
You will need: Shallow supervised water, Pool side
1. Watch the teacher show the supine float and how to stand from it.
2. Practise the supine float while holding the side, then with the arms floating if you are ready.
3. Watch the prone float.
4. Practise a short prone float and stand as soon as you need air.
5. Tell your partner which float felt calmer and why.

## Practice
1. What does supine mean?
2. What does prone mean?
3. Where should the eyes look in a supine float?

## Summary
• Supine: ears in the water, eyes up, mouth clear, body relaxed.
• Prone: face down, body long, stand or turn the head to breathe.
• Practise in the shallow end beside the side.

### Answers to practice
1. Face up, on the back.
2. Face down, on the front.
3. Up, not toward the feet.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Gliding in the water

LESSON 6: GLIDING IN THE WATER
==============================

## What you will learn
• Push off and glide on the front in a long shape.
• Try a short back glide if the front glide is calm.
• Stand up when the glide slows.

Curriculum outcomes: d) glide in water for water confidence

## Introduction
A glide is a float that travels. You push from the side and hold a straight shape while the water carries you a short distance.

## Notes
Gliding builds water confidence because you move without splashing wildly. The body is streamlined: long, tight and straight, like one line.

### Front glide
1. Stand in the shallow end, facing away from the wall, with one foot against the wall if you can reach it comfortably. If you cannot, hold the side, then push gently with both feet from the floor.
2. Arms stretch forward, hands together, squeezing the ears.
3. Take a breath, put the face in if you are ready, and push.
4. Legs stay together, toes pointed.
5. Hold the shape. Do not start swimming strokes yet.
6. When you slow down, stand: knees tuck, feet press the floor, head lifts.

### Back glide
Only try this after the supine float feels calm.

1. Start with the back against the wall, ears ready to rest in the water.
2. Arms stay by the sides or stretched overhead if your teacher prefers.
3. Look up, push gently with the feet, and hold the long shape.
4. Stand by tucking and bringing the head forward.

### Safety
Glide only into empty shallow water. Look before you push so you do not glide into a classmate. One glide at a time in each lane or space. If water goes up the nose, stand, blow gently out of the nose next time, and try a shorter push. A short straight glide is better than a long crooked one.

The glide uses the same posture idea as the floats: a level body moves more cleanly than a bent one.

## Key words
• glide — a push-off in a long shape so the body travels on the water
• streamlined — long and straight so you move through the water more easily

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner glides with the arms by the hips and the knees bent, and barely moves. What shape would help?

Working:
1. A glide should be one long line.
2. Arms forward and legs straight make the body streamlined.

Answer: A straight shape with arms stretched forward, hands together, and legs together.

### Example 2
Two learners push off toward each other. What rule have they broken?

Working:
1. Glide into empty water.
2. Look before you push.

Answer: They glided into a space that was not empty. One person glides at a time into clear shallow water.

## Activity: Push and glide
You will need: Shallow supervised water, A clear space at the wall
1. Watch a front glide and the stand-up.
2. Practise the arm and body shape while holding the side.
3. Push into a short front glide, one learner at a time.
4. Stand, return, and try once more if the first glide was calm.
5. Attempt a short back glide only if your supine float is steady and the teacher agrees.

## Practice
1. What is a glide?
2. Where should the hands be in a front glide?
3. When should you stand up?

## Summary
• Push gently and hold a long, straight shape.
• Glide only into empty shallow water.
• Stand by tucking the knees and pressing the feet down.

### Answers to practice
1. A push-off in a long straight shape so the body travels a short way on the water.
2. Together, stretched forward, squeezing the ears.
3. When the glide slows, or sooner if you need air or the way is not clear.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Practising float and glide with feedback

LESSON 7: PRACTISING FLOAT AND GLIDE WITH FEEDBACK
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Practise one float and one glide you can already start.
• Watch a partner and give safe, respectful feedback.
• Choose one point to improve.

Curriculum outcomes: c) float in water for skill acquisition; d) glide in water for water confidence

## Introduction
Repeating a float without looking at it does not always make it better. A partner at the side can see if your body is tucked, flat or bent, and can tell you without touching you.

## Notes
Choose two skills you have already begun: the mushroom float, the supine float, the prone float, or the glide. Practise the safer one first. For most learners that is the mushroom float or the supine float, then a short front glide.

### A practice set
1. Enter feet first.
2. Perform the float for a short count and stand.
3. Rest for several breaths.
4. Perform a short glide into empty space and stand.
5. Get out of the way so your partner can go.

### Feedback from the deck or the shallows
The partner does not push you, hold you down, or come underneath you. They watch one point only:

- Mushroom: were the knees tucked and did you stand with control?
- Supine: were the ears in and the eyes up?
- Prone: was the body long, and did you lift the head or stand to breathe?
- Glide: were the arms stretched and the path clear?

They say, “I saw…” and “Next time…”. Example: “I saw a tucked mushroom float. Next time, press your feet down sooner when you stand.”

Respect means you do not laugh if a partner stands up quickly. Standing up is a correct safety choice. Self-confidence grows when the class treats a short, calm float as success.

Write the one point you will practise next time. Improving one point is better than trying every skill badly in one lesson.

## Key words
• feedback — a comment about what was done and one way to improve it
• practice set — a planned number of tries with a rest between them

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A partner laughs because a learner stands up after two counts. What is a respectful response instead?

Working:
1. Standing to breathe is correct.
2. Feedback should be kind and specific.

Answer: Example: “I saw you stand safely. Next time, you might hold the tuck for one more count if you still have air.”

### Example 2
A learner plans 4 floats and 2 glides. How many skills performances is that?

Working:
1. 4 + 2 = 6

Answer: 6

## Activity: One float, one glide, one tip
You will need: Shallow supervised water, A partner on the deck or standing nearby
1. Perform your chosen float and stand.
2. Perform one short glide into a clear space and stand.
3. Your partner gives “I saw…” and “Next time…”.
4. Repeat once, thinking about that single tip.
5. Swap roles. Climb out when the whistle blows.

## Practice
1. What must a partner not do during feedback in the water?
2. Why is standing up early acceptable?
3. What two sentences does useful feedback use?

## Summary
• Practise one familiar float and one short glide.
• Partners watch without grabbing.
• Improve one point at a time.

### Answers to practice
1. They must not push you, hold you under, or get in the way of your glide.
2. Needing air or feeling unsafe means standing is the right choice.
3. “I saw…” and “Next time…”.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: Safety in and out of the pool

LESSON 8: SAFETY IN AND OUT OF THE POOL
=======================================

## What you will learn
• List safety rules for the deck, the changing area and the water.
• Explain how pool hygiene protects swimmers.
• Show that you value safety while playing and practising.

Curriculum outcomes: e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## Introduction
The floats and games only stay enjoyable if everyone leaves the pool healthy. Safety is the skill that wraps around every other skill in this sub-strand.

## Notes
Review safety for the whole visit, not only for the moment you are floating.

### Before swimming
- Swim only with a teacher or lifeguard present. Never swim alone.
- Wear suitable swim clothes. Tie long hair.
- Shower before you enter if the pool asks you to. Clean skin keeps the water cleaner.
- Do not swim with an open wound. Do not enter if you have a stomach illness.
- Use the toilet first. The pool is not a toilet.
- Walk on the deck.

### In the water
- Stay in the shallow end unless a qualified adult moves you.
- Enter feet first. Do not dive in these lessons.
- Do not push, duck or grab ankles.
- Glide and float only in a clear space.
- Obey the whistle immediately.
- If you are tired or frightened, go to the side and tell the adult.
- If another person is in difficulty, shout for the adult. Do not climb on them.

### After swimming
- Climb out carefully.
- Shower and dry off.
- Do not run in the changing area.
- Report any cut or bump.

### Why it matters
Pool hygiene and safe behaviour protect the whole class. A game that breaks the rules is not the fun this sub-strand means. Appreciating safety means you keep the rules even when you are excited, and you remind a friend quietly rather than copying a dare.

Swimming remains a life skill because of these habits: calm entry, the ability to float, the ability to reach the side, and the sense to swim only in a safe place with an adult.

## Key words
• pool hygiene — clean habits that keep the water and swimmers healthy
• supervision — an adult watching and in charge

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner wants to practise the glide in a river after school because the pool lesson felt easy. Is that a good plan?

Working:
1. These skills were learnt in a supervised pool.
2. Rivers have currents, unknown depth and no lifeguard.

Answer: No. Practise only in a supervised pool. A river is not the same place.

### Example 2
Name the first action if a classmate slips under and does not stand.

Working:
1. Grade 4 learners do not attempt a rescue by jumping on the person.
2. They call the adult.

Answer: Shout for the teacher or lifeguard at once.

## Activity: Safety charter
You will need: Paper or a board, The pool rules of the school
1. In groups, list rules for before, during and after swimming.
2. Add one hygiene rule and one rule about helping someone in difficulty.
3. Make a short charter and read it to the class.
4. If you are at the pool, enter once more only for a calm feet-first practice and a short float, then exit on the whistle.
5. Say which rule you will remember every visit.

## Practice
1. Give three safety rules for swimming lessons.
2. Give one pool hygiene rule.
3. What do you do if someone is in difficulty?

## Summary
• Swim only with an adult, feet first, in the shallow end.
• Keep the water clean and your hands to yourself.
• Call an adult if there is trouble, and do not practise in rivers or dams.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: swim with an adult, stay in the shallow end, enter feet first, do not dive, do not push or duck others, obey the whistle, do not swim in rivers.
2. Any one: shower before swimming, use the toilet first, do not swim with a stomach illness or open wound, do not urinate in the pool.
3. Shout for the teacher or lifeguard. Do not jump on them.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 2.6 SWIMMING (OPTIONAL)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Where should beginners in this sub-strand practise?
   A. The deep end
   B. A river
   C. The shallow end of a supervised pool
   D. A well

2. Which entry is correct for these lessons?
   A. A dive
   B. A feet-first entry
   C. A flip from the diving board
   D. Being pushed in

3. Why is diving not used here?

4. What is the purpose of the game Collect the floats?
   A. practise diving to the bottom
   B. build confidence while having fun in shallow water
   C. race to the deep end
   D. push friends under

5. If the whistle blows during a game, what should you do?
   A. finish the point first
   B. stop and look at the adult
   C. duck under water
   D. run on the deck

6. A mushroom float looks like…
   A. a long star on the back
   B. a tuck with the knees to the chest
   C. a dive
   D. standing on the deck

7. In a supine float, the eyes should look…
   A. at the toes
   B. up
   C. at the bottom of the pool
   D. at a friend behind you

8. A front glide needs the body to be…
   A. curled in a ball
   B. long and straight, arms forward
   C. sitting on the steps
   D. splashing hard

9. A partner giving feedback must not…
   A. say what they saw
   B. hold the swimmer under the water
   C. suggest one improvement
   D. wait for their own turn

10. If a classmate is in difficulty in the water, what should you do?
   A. jump on them and push them down
   B. shout for the teacher or lifeguard
   C. ignore them and keep playing
   D. tell them to swim to the deep end
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 2.6 SWIMMING (OPTIONAL)
========================================

1. C. The shallow end of a supervised pool
   Skills are learnt where you can stand, with an adult watching.

2. B. A feet-first entry
   The class uses feet-first entries only.

3. A head-first entry can injure the head and neck, especially in shallow water.
   Feet-first entries are the safe method for this level.

4. B. build confidence while having fun in shallow water
   Water games are for fun and confidence, with safety rules.

5. B. stop and look at the adult
   The whistle is a safety signal.

6. B. a tuck with the knees to the chest
   The body is tucked and rounded at the surface.

7. B. up
   Looking up helps the hips stay near the surface.

8. B. long and straight, arms forward
   A streamlined shape lets you travel a short distance.

9. B. hold the swimmer under the water
   Feedback is given without grabbing or pushing anyone under.

10. B. shout for the teacher or lifeguard
   Call the adult. Do not attempt a rescue by climbing on the person.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Swimming is an optional sub-strand for schools that can use a pool safely. You will learn how a pool is organised, how to enter feet first, and how to play simple water games. You will then practise the mushroom, supine and prone floats, and a glide, always with a teacher present and with safety rules in and out of the water.

## Strand 2.0: Performing and Displaying
Sub-strand 2.6: Swimming (Optional)
Suggested lessons: 15

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) recognise ways of water entry in the swimming pool
b) play water games in the swimming pool for fun
c) float in water for skill acquisition
d) glide in water for water confidence
e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## What this sub-strand covers
• Water entry
• Water games
• Floating technique- mushroom supine and prone
• Gliding

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why is Swimming an essential life skill?

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: The learner builds confidence by floating in water
• Learning to learn: The learner acquires the skills of pool entry and floating in water

## Values
• Respect: The learner respects others' performance in floating and gliding in water
• Responsibility: The learner observes own and others safety while performing and practising the water entry, floating and gliding

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Safety and security: The learner adheres to water safety precautions while practising water entry, floating and gliding
• Environmental awareness: The learner familiarises with the pool environment, safe use of water and pool hygiene

## Links to other learning areas
• Science and Technology: The learner develops a practical understanding of correct body posture when floating and gliding

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Creative Arts Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Performing and Displaying, Sub-strand 2.6 Swimming (Optional)

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Knowing the pool and why swimming matters
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: KNOWING THE POOL AND WHY SWIMMING MATTERS
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Name the main parts of a swimming pool area.
• Explain why swimming is a life skill.
• State rules for moving safely on the pool deck.

Curriculum outcomes: a) recognise ways of water entry in the swimming pool; e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## Introduction
The edge of a pool is hard, and the water is not the same depth everywhere. Before anyone floats or plays, the class needs to know the place and the reasons for being careful.

## Notes
A swimming pool is a controlled place to learn water skills. This sub-strand is optional: it is taught where a pool and proper supervision are available. Do not practise these skills in a river, a dam, a well or flood water.

### Parts of the pool area
- The **deck** is the floor around the pool. It is often wet and slippery.
- **Steps or a ladder** are a safe way in and out.
- The **shallow end** is where your class learns. You should be able to stand with your head well above the water.
- The **deep end** is for swimmers the teacher has passed. Stay out of it in these lessons.
- A **lifeguard or teacher** watches the water. Their whistle means stop and look at them.
- **Lane ropes** and markers divide the water. Do not hang on ropes unless you are told to.

### Why swimming is a life skill
Water is part of ordinary life: baths, rain, rivers and pools. A person who can enter water calmly, float and reach the side has a better chance of staying safe if they fall in. Swimming also builds fitness, breath control and confidence. It is enjoyable. At Grade 4 you are beginning that skill, not training to rescue other people. If someone is in trouble, you shout for an adult. You do not jump in to be a hero.

### On the deck
Walk. Do not run, push or dive. Shower if the pool rules say so. Listen before you go near the edge. These habits are the start of safety in and out of the pool.

## Key words
• deck — the floor around the swimming pool
• shallow end — the part of the pool where you can stand safely
• life skill — a skill that can protect you in real life

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner runs along the wet deck. What is the danger, and what should they do instead?

Working:
1. Wet decks are slippery.
2. Running can cause a fall onto a hard surface or into the water.

Answer: They may slip and be hurt. They should walk.

### Example 2
Why is swimming called a life skill?

Working:
1. It helps a person stay safer in water.
2. It also builds fitness and confidence.

Answer: It helps you stay calm and safer if you are in water, and it keeps the body fit.

## Activity: Pool walk and rules
You will need: A supervised swimming pool, Whistle, Swim clothes
1. With the teacher, walk the deck and point to the shallow end, the deep end, the steps and the lifeguard’s place.
2. Practise stopping still when the whistle blows.
3. In pairs, say one reason swimming is a life skill.
4. Agree three deck rules and repeat them aloud.
5. Do not enter the water until the teacher gives the instruction.

## Practice
1. Where should Grade 4 beginners stay in the pool?
2. What does a whistle from the teacher or lifeguard mean?
3. Give two deck rules.

## Summary
• Learn the deck, the steps, the shallow end and the deep end.
• Swimming can keep you safer in water and makes you fitter.
• Walk on the deck and obey the whistle.

### Answers to practice
1. In the shallow end, where they can stand, with a teacher watching.
2. Stop and look at the adult.
3. Any two: walk, do not push, do not dive, listen to the adult, shower if required.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Entering the water feet first
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: ENTERING THE WATER FEET FIRST
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Enter the pool using steps and a feet-first method.
• Explain why this class does not dive.
• Get out of the pool safely when told.

Curriculum outcomes: a) recognise ways of water entry in the swimming pool; e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## Introduction
How you enter the water is a skill of its own. In this class the rule is simple: feet first, and only where the teacher has told you to enter.

## Notes
There is more than one safe way into a pool. All of the ways you use now put the feet in first. You do not dive. Diving into water that is shallow, or into water you have not checked, can injure the head and the neck.

### Ways to enter
1. **Steps or ladder.** Face the steps, hold the rail, and walk down one step at a time until you are standing on the pool floor. This is the first method to master.
2. **Sitting entry.** Sit on the edge where the teacher shows you. Both hands hold the edge. Turn your body, slide in, and land on your feet. Keep your head up.
3. **Feet-first jump.** Use this only when the teacher points to a place where you can stand afterwards and where jumping is allowed. Bend your knees, look forward, jump so the feet go in first, and let the knees bend again as you land in the water. Do not leap far out into the pool. Do not jump onto another person.

Never enter by flipping, diving, or being pushed.

### Getting out
Swim or walk to the steps and climb out, or place both hands on the edge, push down and climb onto a knee. Do not pull on another learner. When the whistle says the turn is over, get out at once.

### Safety around entry
One person enters at a time at each entry point. Wait a body-length away from the person in front. Keep your eyes on the water where you will land. If you feel afraid, say so. Using the steps is a successful entry. Confidence grows from calm practice, not from a dare.

## Key words
• feet-first — entering the water with the feet going in before the head
• dive — going in head first; not allowed in these lessons

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The shallow end is busy and a friend says, “Dive at the deep end so you look brave.” What should you do?

Working:
1. This class enters feet first only.
2. The deep end is not the learning area.

Answer: Refuse. Enter feet first at the place the teacher has given you.

### Example 2
Three learners want to use the ladder at once. What is the safe number at a time?

Working:
1. One person enters at each entry point at a time.

Answer: One.

## Activity: Feet-first entries
You will need: Supervised pool, Steps or ladder, Teacher or lifeguard
1. Watch the teacher demonstrate the steps, the sitting entry and, if the depth is safe, a feet-first jump.
2. Enter one at a time by the steps and stand in the shallow water.
3. Get out and, if you are ready, practise the sitting entry.
4. Try a feet-first jump only where the teacher stands and only if you agree you are ready.
5. Climb out safely when the whistle blows.

## Practice
1. Name two feet-first ways to enter a pool.
2. Why do you not dive in this sub-strand?
3. How many learners should use the ladder at the same time?

## Summary
• Enter on the steps, by sliding in from sitting, or with a feet-first jump if allowed.
• Do not dive or push anyone in.
• Get out on the steps or by climbing onto a knee when told.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: steps or ladder, sitting entry, feet-first jump where the teacher allows it.
2. Diving is head first and can injure the head and neck, especially in shallow water.
3. One.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Water games for confidence
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: WATER GAMES FOR CONFIDENCE
====================================

## What you will learn
• Play simple games in shallow water.
• Follow safety rules while playing.
• Explain how games help you feel at home in the water.

Curriculum outcomes: b) play water games in the swimming pool for fun; e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## Introduction
Games in shallow water are not a break from learning. They teach you to move, watch others and listen to the whistle while you are having fun.

## Notes
Water games in this lesson stay in the shallow end. You can stand up at any moment. An adult is watching. The games are for confidence and enjoyment, not for rough play.

### Game 1: Walk and greet
Walk across the shallow end, shoulders under the water if you are tall enough for that to be safe, and give a partner a calm high-five. Change direction when the whistle blows. This teaches you to move without grabbing.

### Game 2: Collect the floats
The teacher floats a few safe objects, such as balls, on the water. In turns, walk or paddle and bring one object back to the side. No diving down. If an object sinks, leave it for the teacher.

### Game 3: Statues
Move gently through the water until the whistle blows, then freeze. A freeze might be standing still, or holding the side. Pushing someone who is a statue is not part of the game.

### Safety inside the game
- Stay in the area the teacher marked.
- Keep your feet under you unless the teacher has asked for a float.
- Do not duck another person’s head under the water.
- Do not run on the spot so wildly that you slip.
- Leave the game the moment the whistle sounds, even if you are about to collect a ball.
- Help a friend who is nervous by staying near them, not by pulling them.

These games make the pool feel familiar. Familiar water is safer water, because you are not panicking at the cold, the splash or the space. Fun and safety are practised together.

## Key words
• water confidence — feeling calm and able to follow instructions in the water
• shallow-end game — a game played where you can stand safely

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During Collect the floats, a ball sinks. What should a learner do?

Working:
1. The lesson says not to dive down.
2. An adult collects sunken objects.

Answer: Leave it for the teacher. Do not dive down.

### Example 2
Why must the game stop when the whistle blows, even if you are winning?

Working:
1. The whistle is a safety signal.
2. Safety is more important than the point.

Answer: The whistle means stop and look at the adult. Safety comes before the game.

## Activity: Three shallow-water games
You will need: Supervised shallow water, Whistle, A few floating balls
1. Enter feet first and stand where you can touch the floor.
2. Play Walk and greet, stopping on the whistle.
3. Play Collect the floats in turns.
4. Play Statues without pushing.
5. Climb out, and tell a partner which game helped you feel calmer in the water.

## Practice
1. Name one water game for the shallow end.
2. What must you never do to another person’s head during a water game?
3. Why are water games useful?

## Summary
• Play in the shallow end where you can stand.
• Do not duck heads, dive for sunk objects, or ignore the whistle.
• Games make the water familiar and enjoyable.

### Answers to practice
1. Any one: Walk and greet, Collect the floats, or Statues.
2. Push it under the water.
3. They build confidence and enjoyment while you practise moving safely and listening.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: The mushroom float
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: THE MUSHROOM FLOAT
============================

## What you will learn
• Describe the shape of a mushroom float.
• Practise the float in shallow water with support nearby.
• Stand up from the float with control.

Curriculum outcomes: c) float in water for skill acquisition

## Introduction
A mushroom float curls the body into a round shape so the water can hold you for a moment. It is often the first float learners trust, because the knees are tucked and the face is near the surface.

## Notes
Floating means resting in the water so the body is held up without standing. The mushroom float is also called a tuck float. The back rounds near the surface like the cap of a mushroom, and the knees are tucked underneath.

### How to do it
1. Stand in the shallow end where your feet can push the floor.
2. Take a breath.
3. Bend the knees and pull them toward the chest.
4. Hold the shins with the hands.
5. Round the back and let the body tip forward gently. The face may go into the water for a short moment if you are ready. If you are not ready, keep the chin near the water and the face to the side, and tell the teacher. Do not force the face in.
6. Stay tucked and relaxed. Tight, panicked muscles make you sink.
7. To stand: lift the head, press the feet down to the floor, and stand tall. The teacher or a partner may stand beside you, but they do not hold you under.

Practise near the side so you can touch it. One learner floats at a time in each small space. Count a short hold, such as three counts, then stand. As you improve, the hold can grow.

The mushroom float teaches you that water can support a calm body. It is a skill for confidence. It is not a test of how long you can stay without breath. If you need air, stand up at once.

## Key words
• mushroom float — a tucked float with the knees to the chest and the back rounded at the surface
• float — to rest in the water so it holds you up

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner holds a mushroom float for 3 counts, stands, and does it again for 3 counts. How many counts were spent floating?

Working:
1. 3 + 3 = 6

Answer: 6

### Example 2
A learner feels they need air during the float. What should they do?

Working:
1. Breath matters more than the hold.
2. The recovery is to stand.

Answer: Stand up at once by lifting the head and pressing the feet to the floor.

## Activity: Tuck and float
You will need: Shallow supervised water, Pool side within reach
1. Watch a demonstration of the mushroom float and the stand-up.
2. Hold the side, tuck the knees, and round the back for a short count.
3. Let go only if you feel ready, with a partner beside you but not holding you down.
4. Stand up with control.
5. Tell your partner one thing that helped you float.

## Practice
1. What shape is the body in a mushroom float?
2. How do you stand up from the float?
3. Should you force your face into the water if you are afraid?

## Summary
• Tuck the knees, hold the shins and round the back.
• Relax, hold briefly, then stand by pressing the feet down.
• Stay in shallow water and stop when you need air.

### Answers to practice
1. Tucked and round, knees to the chest, back near the surface.
2. Lift the head, press the feet to the floor and stand tall.
3. No. Keep the face to the side until you are ready, and tell the teacher.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Supine and prone floats
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: SUPINE AND PRONE FLOATS
=================================

## What you will learn
• Float on the back in a supine float.
• Float face down in a prone float, with a safe way to breathe.
• Compare the two body positions.

Curriculum outcomes: c) float in water for skill acquisition

## Introduction
The mushroom float tucks you into a ball. The next floats stretch you out. Supine means face up. Prone means face down. Both need a calm body and shallow water.

## Notes
### Supine float
Supine means lying on the back.

1. Hold the pool side with both hands, arms bent.
2. Lift the hips and let the chest rise so the ears rest in the water.
3. Look up at the sky or the roof, not at your feet. Looking at the feet makes the hips sink.
4. When you are ready, let the arms float out to the sides, like a letter T.
5. Keep the legs relaxed. A small kick is allowed if the teacher has shown it, but the aim is to rest, not to race.
6. Breathe normally. The mouth stays clear of the water.
7. To stand: tuck the knees, bring the head forward and press the feet down.

### Prone float
Prone means face down, on the front.

1. Face the side and hold it.
2. Take a breath and place the face in the water if you are ready, arms stretched forward or out.
3. Let the legs trail. The body is long, a little like a star if the arms and legs are spread.
4. To breathe, lift the head or turn it to the side, or stand up.
5. Do not stay face down if you feel short of air.

### What the two floats teach
Supine lets you breathe more easily, so many learners gain confidence there first. Prone teaches you to put the face in and to stretch long, which you will need for a front glide. In both, a tight, frightened body sinks faster than a relaxed one. Practise beside the side, one person in each space, with the teacher watching.

Science link: a long, level body lies better on the water than a body folded at the hips. Posture is part of floating.

## Key words
• supine float — a back float, face up
• prone float — a front float, face down

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During a back float, a learner looks down toward the toes and the hips sink. What should they look at?

Working:
1. Looking at the feet drops the hips.
2. The eyes should look up.

Answer: They should look up, with the ears in the water.

### Example 2
Which float makes breathing easier for a beginner, supine or prone? Why?

Working:
1. Supine is face up.
2. The mouth can stay out of the water.

Answer: Supine, because the face is up and the mouth can stay clear of the water.

## Activity: Back float and front float
You will need: Shallow supervised water, Pool side
1. Watch the teacher show the supine float and how to stand from it.
2. Practise the supine float while holding the side, then with the arms floating if you are ready.
3. Watch the prone float.
4. Practise a short prone float and stand as soon as you need air.
5. Tell your partner which float felt calmer and why.

## Practice
1. What does supine mean?
2. What does prone mean?
3. Where should the eyes look in a supine float?

## Summary
• Supine: ears in the water, eyes up, mouth clear, body relaxed.
• Prone: face down, body long, stand or turn the head to breathe.
• Practise in the shallow end beside the side.

### Answers to practice
1. Face up, on the back.
2. Face down, on the front.
3. Up, not toward the feet.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Gliding in the water
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: GLIDING IN THE WATER
==============================

## What you will learn
• Push off and glide on the front in a long shape.
• Try a short back glide if the front glide is calm.
• Stand up when the glide slows.

Curriculum outcomes: d) glide in water for water confidence

## Introduction
A glide is a float that travels. You push from the side and hold a straight shape while the water carries you a short distance.

## Notes
Gliding builds water confidence because you move without splashing wildly. The body is streamlined: long, tight and straight, like one line.

### Front glide
1. Stand in the shallow end, facing away from the wall, with one foot against the wall if you can reach it comfortably. If you cannot, hold the side, then push gently with both feet from the floor.
2. Arms stretch forward, hands together, squeezing the ears.
3. Take a breath, put the face in if you are ready, and push.
4. Legs stay together, toes pointed.
5. Hold the shape. Do not start swimming strokes yet.
6. When you slow down, stand: knees tuck, feet press the floor, head lifts.

### Back glide
Only try this after the supine float feels calm.

1. Start with the back against the wall, ears ready to rest in the water.
2. Arms stay by the sides or stretched overhead if your teacher prefers.
3. Look up, push gently with the feet, and hold the long shape.
4. Stand by tucking and bringing the head forward.

### Safety
Glide only into empty shallow water. Look before you push so you do not glide into a classmate. One glide at a time in each lane or space. If water goes up the nose, stand, blow gently out of the nose next time, and try a shorter push. A short straight glide is better than a long crooked one.

The glide uses the same posture idea as the floats: a level body moves more cleanly than a bent one.

## Key words
• glide — a push-off in a long shape so the body travels on the water
• streamlined — long and straight so you move through the water more easily

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner glides with the arms by the hips and the knees bent, and barely moves. What shape would help?

Working:
1. A glide should be one long line.
2. Arms forward and legs straight make the body streamlined.

Answer: A straight shape with arms stretched forward, hands together, and legs together.

### Example 2
Two learners push off toward each other. What rule have they broken?

Working:
1. Glide into empty water.
2. Look before you push.

Answer: They glided into a space that was not empty. One person glides at a time into clear shallow water.

## Activity: Push and glide
You will need: Shallow supervised water, A clear space at the wall
1. Watch a front glide and the stand-up.
2. Practise the arm and body shape while holding the side.
3. Push into a short front glide, one learner at a time.
4. Stand, return, and try once more if the first glide was calm.
5. Attempt a short back glide only if your supine float is steady and the teacher agrees.

## Practice
1. What is a glide?
2. Where should the hands be in a front glide?
3. When should you stand up?

## Summary
• Push gently and hold a long, straight shape.
• Glide only into empty shallow water.
• Stand by tucking the knees and pressing the feet down.

### Answers to practice
1. A push-off in a long straight shape so the body travels a short way on the water.
2. Together, stretched forward, squeezing the ears.
3. When the glide slows, or sooner if you need air or the way is not clear.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Practising float and glide with feedback
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: PRACTISING FLOAT AND GLIDE WITH FEEDBACK
==================================================

## What you will learn
• Practise one float and one glide you can already start.
• Watch a partner and give safe, respectful feedback.
• Choose one point to improve.

Curriculum outcomes: c) float in water for skill acquisition; d) glide in water for water confidence

## Introduction
Repeating a float without looking at it does not always make it better. A partner at the side can see if your body is tucked, flat or bent, and can tell you without touching you.

## Notes
Choose two skills you have already begun: the mushroom float, the supine float, the prone float, or the glide. Practise the safer one first. For most learners that is the mushroom float or the supine float, then a short front glide.

### A practice set
1. Enter feet first.
2. Perform the float for a short count and stand.
3. Rest for several breaths.
4. Perform a short glide into empty space and stand.
5. Get out of the way so your partner can go.

### Feedback from the deck or the shallows
The partner does not push you, hold you down, or come underneath you. They watch one point only:

- Mushroom: were the knees tucked and did you stand with control?
- Supine: were the ears in and the eyes up?
- Prone: was the body long, and did you lift the head or stand to breathe?
- Glide: were the arms stretched and the path clear?

They say, “I saw…” and “Next time…”. Example: “I saw a tucked mushroom float. Next time, press your feet down sooner when you stand.”

Respect means you do not laugh if a partner stands up quickly. Standing up is a correct safety choice. Self-confidence grows when the class treats a short, calm float as success.

Write the one point you will practise next time. Improving one point is better than trying every skill badly in one lesson.

## Key words
• feedback — a comment about what was done and one way to improve it
• practice set — a planned number of tries with a rest between them

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A partner laughs because a learner stands up after two counts. What is a respectful response instead?

Working:
1. Standing to breathe is correct.
2. Feedback should be kind and specific.

Answer: Example: “I saw you stand safely. Next time, you might hold the tuck for one more count if you still have air.”

### Example 2
A learner plans 4 floats and 2 glides. How many skills performances is that?

Working:
1. 4 + 2 = 6

Answer: 6

## Activity: One float, one glide, one tip
You will need: Shallow supervised water, A partner on the deck or standing nearby
1. Perform your chosen float and stand.
2. Perform one short glide into a clear space and stand.
3. Your partner gives “I saw…” and “Next time…”.
4. Repeat once, thinking about that single tip.
5. Swap roles. Climb out when the whistle blows.

## Practice
1. What must a partner not do during feedback in the water?
2. Why is standing up early acceptable?
3. What two sentences does useful feedback use?

## Summary
• Practise one familiar float and one short glide.
• Partners watch without grabbing.
• Improve one point at a time.

### Answers to practice
1. They must not push you, hold you under, or get in the way of your glide.
2. Needing air or feeling unsafe means standing is the right choice.
3. “I saw…” and “Next time…”.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Safety in and out of the pool
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: SAFETY IN AND OUT OF THE POOL
=======================================

## What you will learn
• List safety rules for the deck, the changing area and the water.
• Explain how pool hygiene protects swimmers.
• Show that you value safety while playing and practising.

Curriculum outcomes: e) appreciate safety in and out of the swimming pool while playing water games

## Introduction
The floats and games only stay enjoyable if everyone leaves the pool healthy. Safety is the skill that wraps around every other skill in this sub-strand.

## Notes
Review safety for the whole visit, not only for the moment you are floating.

### Before swimming
- Swim only with a teacher or lifeguard present. Never swim alone.
- Wear suitable swim clothes. Tie long hair.
- Shower before you enter if the pool asks you to. Clean skin keeps the water cleaner.
- Do not swim with an open wound. Do not enter if you have a stomach illness.
- Use the toilet first. The pool is not a toilet.
- Walk on the deck.

### In the water
- Stay in the shallow end unless a qualified adult moves you.
- Enter feet first. Do not dive in these lessons.
- Do not push, duck or grab ankles.
- Glide and float only in a clear space.
- Obey the whistle immediately.
- If you are tired or frightened, go to the side and tell the adult.
- If another person is in difficulty, shout for the adult. Do not climb on them.

### After swimming
- Climb out carefully.
- Shower and dry off.
- Do not run in the changing area.
- Report any cut or bump.

### Why it matters
Pool hygiene and safe behaviour protect the whole class. A game that breaks the rules is not the fun this sub-strand means. Appreciating safety means you keep the rules even when you are excited, and you remind a friend quietly rather than copying a dare.

Swimming remains a life skill because of these habits: calm entry, the ability to float, the ability to reach the side, and the sense to swim only in a safe place with an adult.

## Key words
• pool hygiene — clean habits that keep the water and swimmers healthy
• supervision — an adult watching and in charge

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner wants to practise the glide in a river after school because the pool lesson felt easy. Is that a good plan?

Working:
1. These skills were learnt in a supervised pool.
2. Rivers have currents, unknown depth and no lifeguard.

Answer: No. Practise only in a supervised pool. A river is not the same place.

### Example 2
Name the first action if a classmate slips under and does not stand.

Working:
1. Grade 4 learners do not attempt a rescue by jumping on the person.
2. They call the adult.

Answer: Shout for the teacher or lifeguard at once.

## Activity: Safety charter
You will need: Paper or a board, The pool rules of the school
1. In groups, list rules for before, during and after swimming.
2. Add one hygiene rule and one rule about helping someone in difficulty.
3. Make a short charter and read it to the class.
4. If you are at the pool, enter once more only for a calm feet-first practice and a short float, then exit on the whistle.
5. Say which rule you will remember every visit.

## Practice
1. Give three safety rules for swimming lessons.
2. Give one pool hygiene rule.
3. What do you do if someone is in difficulty?

## Summary
• Swim only with an adult, feet first, in the shallow end.
• Keep the water clean and your hands to yourself.
• Call an adult if there is trouble, and do not practise in rivers or dams.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: swim with an adult, stay in the shallow end, enter feet first, do not dive, do not push or duck others, obey the whistle, do not swim in rivers.
2. Any one: shower before swimming, use the toilet first, do not swim with a stomach illness or open wound, do not urinate in the pool.
3. Shout for the teacher or lifeguard. Do not jump on them.

questions.question: Where should beginners in this sub-strand practise?
options: The shallow end of a supervised pool
questions.explanation: Skills are learnt where you can stand, with an adult watching.

questions.question: Which entry is correct for these lessons?
options: A flip from the diving board
questions.explanation: The class uses feet-first entries only.

questions.question: Why is diving not used here?
questions.answer: A head-first entry can injure the head and neck, especially in shallow water.
questions.explanation: Feet-first entries are the safe method for this level.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the game Collect the floats?
options: build confidence while having fun in shallow water
questions.explanation: Water games are for fun and confidence, with safety rules.

questions.question: If the whistle blows during a game, what should you do?
options: stop and look at the adult
questions.explanation: The whistle is a safety signal.

questions.question: A mushroom float looks like…
options: a long star on the back
a tuck with the knees to the chest
questions.explanation: The body is tucked and rounded at the surface.

questions.question: In a supine float, the eyes should look…
options: at the bottom of the pool
questions.explanation: Looking up helps the hips stay near the surface.

questions.question: A front glide needs the body to be…
questions.explanation: A streamlined shape lets you travel a short distance.

questions.question: A partner giving feedback must not…
options: hold the swimmer under the water
questions.explanation: Feedback is given without grabbing or pushing anyone under.

questions.question: If a classmate is in difficulty in the water, what should you do?
options: jump on them and push them down
shout for the teacher or lifeguard
tell them to swim to the deep end
questions.explanation: Call the adult. Do not attempt a rescue by climbing on the person.
